How I approach automation

I don't start with the tool — I start with the step a person shouldn't have to do by hand anymore. Once that's clear, AI and automation are just the fastest way to build the fix: a script, a form, a dashboard, a model. The judgment call — what to automate, what stays human — is the actual work. That's the part I want to keep getting better at.

Understand the process before touching a tool

I map the process before touching technology. Automating the wrong workflow only makes inefficiency happen faster.

Build small, get feedback, then improve

I aim for a working MVP first, not a finished system on the first try. Real feedback from the person who'll use it beats guessing what they need.

I plan the logic, AI writes the code

I design the solution. AI accelerates implementation — not the thinking.

Every output gets checked before it ships

I read and test what AI produces the same way I would a teammate's work. If I can't explain why it's right, it doesn't go to a client.

Santander Bank · Operation Planning & Analysis Intern · Summer 2026

An intake form that thinks along with the person filling it out

A thin, easy-to-skip request form→Power Apps form with a built-in AI assistant
Problem

A New Work Request form already existed on another platform, but it wasn't getting relationship managers what they needed — executives would submit an idea with too little detail to act on, which just pushed the back-and-forth into email instead of eliminating it.

Approach

Rebuilt the form in Power Apps and layered in an AI assistant that engages the executive while they fill it out — asking clarifying questions, helping them think through what they're actually requesting, and prompting for the specific details a relationship manager (RM) would need before it lets a thin request through.

Impact

Requests now arrive with enough detail for RMs to act on the first time, cutting out the round of follow-up emails the original form couldn't prevent.

Santander Bank · Operation Planning & Analysis Intern · Summer 2026

Letting a relationship manager answer "how close is my idea?" in one lookup

PMs manually writing docs & planning reminders→Jira automation rules
Status-check meetings to track IT deployment→Power BI dashboard
Problem

Nothing connected demand to delivery, so a relationship manager (RM) couldn't tell a business executive how close their idea actually was to shipping without chasing down PMs across systems. Every business idea starts as a demand number, which can branch into features, break into stories, and ship inside a release alongside unrelated work.

Approach

Connected 3 separate data sources into Power BI through API calls and modeled the full demand → feature → story → release chain, then built three role-specific dashboards on top of it: a project manager view, an RM view, and a calendar view of upcoming releases.

Impact

An RM can now look up a single demand number and see exactly which stories tied to it are being released and when — turning "how close is this to done?" from a cross-team chase into a lookup.

Consulting Project for Pinecrest Cemetery · ACU · Spring 2026

Turning a 1956 paper ledger into a live plot map

Paper ledger, no record of what's sold or open→Interactive plot map, live below
Problem

A family-owned cemetery had operated entirely on paper since 1956 — no digital record of which plots were available, sold, or in use, and no modern intake, payment, or contract process.

Approach

Led two 4-person teams to diagnose operational gaps and build a modernization roadmap: CRM implementation (HoneyBook), workflow redesign, electronic payments, contract e-signatures, and e-notarization — plus a dynamically updatable plot map (built with AI assistance) that turns raw plot records into a color-coded, searchable diagram of the whole cemetery.

Impact

Delivered the organization's first real-time visual inventory system. The client confirmed intent to implement every recommendation in the roadmap.

ACU AI Analytics Consulting · Spring 2025 – Spring 2026

An auto-grading engine that gave a professor 4 hours back per exam

Checking every answer by hand, exam after exam→Automatic grading system
Problem

A statistics course needed exams graded every 2–3 weeks for around 80 students. Each exam had multiple questions, and each question needed several numeric answers checked — things like the mean, standard deviation, or confidence interval bounds — all done by hand for every student.

Approach

Led a 2-analyst team to build an auto-grading system in Excel: a reference answer key lists what each field on the exam should be, and the underlying code pulls in every student's submitted exam, checks their answers against that key and a points rubric, and records the results — no manual comparison required.

Impact

Cut grading time by 4 hours per exam.

The master key — every field the macro checks, tagged with a keyword and the computed correct value

USME (US Med-Equip) · Data Science Consultant Intern · Spring 2026

A 3-model forecasting bake-off that turned a demand guess into a $6M business case

Guessing equipment demand per branch→SARIMAX / Holt-Winters / RNN forecasts
Problem

USME rents medical equipment (ventilators, monitoring, respiratory, infusion) across branch locations and couldn't reliably answer: how many units of a given model will be requested for rental or pickup in the next 7/14/30 days? Under-forecasting means turning a customer down; over-forecasting ties up inventory that could be allocated elsewhere.

The raw data itself was a problem before modeling could start: 1.6M rows across 35 columns, with 350,000 blank values in the end-date field alone.

Approach

Cleaned and bounded the dataset to a usable time window, then built and benchmarked three forecasting approaches per branch/model-type against a seasonal-naive baseline: SARIMAX (seasonal ARIMA with a 52-week cycle), Holt-Winters exponential smoothing, and an RNN/LSTM (~700 lines of Python across data prep, model training, and evaluation). Evaluated each at 1, 2, 4, and 12-week horizons using RMSE, MAE, and MAPE.

Impact

SARIMAX beat the baseline forecast by 6–31 percentage points of MAPE in a lower-volume market (Pittsburgh) and by 107–127 points in a higher-volume one (Baltimore) — a large enough accuracy gap to act on. Presented findings and a turndown-cost business case to stakeholders as part of a 4-person team.

~$6M/year in reclaimable revenue from better-timed inventory allocation

Personal Project · 2026

An interactive tool to decide which car actually costs less to own

Comparing 4 cars' quotes by hand→Interactive cost comparison, live below
Problem

Deciding between four real options — a RAV4 Woodland, a RAV4 XSE, a new Lexus NX 350h, and a used NX 350h — meant tracking a full 80,000-mile maintenance schedule per car (oil changes, tires, brakes, hybrid-specific service, complimentary-maintenance windows) across separate dealer quotes and owner's manuals. Not something you can eyeball and compare fairly.

Approach

Built a self-contained tool that models purchase price (adjustable per car via sliders, reflecting real market ranges) plus the full maintenance schedule for each car out to 80k miles, then rolls it into one total cost of ownership — visualized as ranked cost bars, a side-by-side summary, and a full service-by-service schedule table.

Impact

Turned four scattered estimates into one live comparison that names the lowest-total-cost option and recalculates instantly as any price assumption changes — the actual tool used to make the purchase decision, not a write-up after the fact.
